report:
## Conclusion

There is **preliminary but limited evidence supporting the claim** that acupuncture can reduce depression symptoms during pregnancy, though it falls short of definitive proof.

The key evidence is Manber et al.'s (2010) randomized controlled trial of 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder, which compared depression-specific acupuncture against control acupuncture and massage. The study found a meaningfully higher response rate (~20% higher) with depression-specific acupuncture compared to controls, and the authors concluded that "the short acupuncture protocol demonstrated symptom reduction and a response rate comparable to those observed in standard depression treatments of similar length and could be a viable treatment option for depression during pregnancy" (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/10.1097/aog.0b013e3181cc0816~acupuncture-for-depression-during-pregnancy-a-randomized). Stanford's coverage of this same trial similarly reports that "acupuncture appears to be an effective way to reduce depression symptoms during pregnancy" (https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2010/02/acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-during-pregnancy-study-shows.html).

However, this remains a single trial, and researchers have been cautious about overgeneralizing. Lead author Rachel Manber herself noted, "I don't think we have a universal conclusion at this point that acupuncture works for depression, but we do have some evidence that's growing" (https://health.usnews.com/health-news/blogs/on-women/2010/02/22/acupuncture-may-help-alleviate-depression-during-pregnancy). A broader meta-analysis on treatments for antenatal depression found "positive results" for acupuncture as an adjunct approach, but emphasized this is alongside more established options like CBT (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0173397).

**Bottom line:** Acupuncture shows promise as an adjunct treatment for antenatal depression based on one solid RCT, but more replication is needed before it can be considered an established, evidence-based standard treatment.
